name: Abilities
content:
ABILITIES are special capabilities that set characters apart from one another. Abilities encompass a very wide range of effects and mechanics, but all are defined within a shared set of concepts:

ABILITY CONCEPTS

ACTION TYPES

An ability's ACTION TYPE defines when and how it can be used:

  • Trait. A passive Ability that is always in effect. Traits themselves do not require activation, but may contain effects within their descriptions that require activation and/or have costs.

  • Action. Requires spending one Action on your turn to activate.

  • Half Action. Requires spending one Half Action on your turn to activate.

  • Free Action. Can be activated at any time, regardless of whose turn it is, without spending any Actions or Reactions.

  • Reaction. Activated in response to a specific triggering event defined in the Ability's description. Reactions can be used at any time, regardless of whose turn it is. See Reactions below.

  • Ritual. Requires extended time and preparation to perform, as specified in the Ability's description.

MESTIERE POINTS

Most Abilities come from your Mestiere, or adventuring discipline (see Character Creation). Just as each Mestiere varies in its approach to adventuring and the Skills it leverages, MESTIERE POINTS (MP) represent different concepts for each Mestiere: physical momentum, chaos on the battlefield, arcane energy, force of will, spiritual vitality - all of these concepts are abstracted as Mestiere Points, the resource that powers Abilities.

Many Abilities have a cost — a number of MP that must be spent to activate them. If an Ability has no MP cost listed, it costs nothing to activate beyond its action type requirement.

How a character generates and manages MP depends on their Mestiere:

  • Spend-Down MP. Most Mestieri grant a maximum MP value. Characters are created with a full pool and spend MP to activate Abilities. MP is partially restored on a Short Rest and fully restored on a Long Rest (see Rest & Recovery).

  • Accumulator MP. Some Mestieri have a maximum MP of 0 and instead earn MP during combat, as defined in their Abilities.

These types are not explicitly defined. Rather they are implicit in the mechanics of each Mestiere.

Regardless of your Mestiere, any MP in excess of your maximum is lost after one minute spent out of combat.

CONCENTRATION

Some abilities are marked CONCENTRATION with a maximum duration — for example, "Concentration, up to 1 minute." A Concentration ability's effect persists for as long as it is actively sustained, up to the stated duration.

Sustaining a Concentration effect costs one Half Action on each of your turns. It is possible to sustain any number of multiple Concentration effects simultaneously, as long as you have the actions available to do so.

If you take damage while Concentrating on any number of abilities, roll Fortitude against a Difficulty equal to the total damage taken. On a pass, you continue Concentrating. On a failure, all Concentration effects immediately end.

Additionally, Concentration ends immediately under any of the following conditions:

  • You choose to end it, as a Free Action.

  • You suffer any amount of Injury.

  • You suffer a Bout of Madness.

REACTIONS

Abilities with the Reaction action type include a Trigger statement in their description. When the trigger event occurs, the you may use that Ability immediately, even if it is not your turn. Triggers appear at the top of the description in the form: "Trigger: [event]."

By default, you have one Reaction per round. Some Abilities may grant additional Reactions; if so, those additional Reactions may be spent on separate triggering events, or on multiple reactions to a single event. Any number of creatures may react to the same triggering event — each spends their own Reaction independently, and they are resolved in "last in, first out" order.

For example, if a triggering event occurs and one character activates Reaction A, then another character activates Reaction B in response, Reaction B is resolved first, then Reaction A.

IMPROVEMENTS

Some Abilities offer IMPROVEMENTS — additional upgrades for that Ability, each with its own description and XP cost. Owning the base ability is a prerequisite for purchasing any of its Improvements. Improvements are purchased via the standard XP spending rules (see Character Advancement).

A character may purchase any number of Improvements for the same Ability. Each Improvement stacks with the base Ability and with any other Improvements already purchased — Improvements do not replace the base Ability's effects unless otherwise stated.

DURATION

If an Ability does not define a duration for an effect, the effect is instantaneous. If an Ability defines a duration for an effect without Concentration, the effects lasts for the stated duration without any further effort required.

Most descriptions of duration are self explanatory: "For the next minute," "For up to 1 hour," etc.

Some effects indicate a duration in units of "rounds." This refers to rounds of combat, and is linked to the turn during which the effect is put into place:

Example 1: You activate an effect that lasts for 1 round on your turn. That effect remains in place until the beginning of your next turn.

Example 2: You activate an effect that lasts for for 1 round as a Reaction during an opponent's turn. That effect remains in place until the beginning of that opponent's next turn (regardless of who the effect targets).

Example 3: You activate an effect that lasts for 3 rounds on your turn. That effect remains in place until the beginning of your third turn after this one.

This shorthand is in place to avoid frequent repetitions of lengthy phrases like, "until the beginning of your next turn," etc., in an effort to make spell descriptions more concise and readable.

Note that, because combatants can choose to order their turns as they like within their group (see Combat), there are often strategic considerations to make when effects with round-specific durations are in play.

PER-USE LIMITS

Ability descriptions often include a frequency limit on use:

  • Once per round. Resets at the start of your next turn.

  • Once per rest. Resets after either a Short Rest or a Long Rest.

  • Once per day. Resets at each sunrise.

  • Once per Quest. Resets only at the start of a new Quest.

THE "VS" NOTATION

Ability descriptions use the notation "[Skill] vs [target]" to indicate how a Check is resolved:

  • When the target is a Skill (e.g., Dexterity vs Dexterity), both parties roll — it is an Opposed Skill Check, and the outcome is described as a win or loss.

  • When the target is a stat or other fixed value (e.g., Strength vs Defense), only one party rolls and compares against that value as the Difficulty — it is a standard Skill Check, and the outcome is described as a pass or fail.

WIN, LOSS, PASS & FAIL

Ability descriptions use this terminology when referring to check outcomes:

  • Pass / Fail. Used when a check is made against a Difficulty. Pass means the result met or exceeded the Difficulty; fail means it did not. Often this is rendered as "On a pass..." or "On a failure..."

  • Win / Lose. Used when a check is an Opposed Skill Check. Win means your result was higher than your opponent's; lose means it was lower. Often this is rendered as "On a win..." or "On a loss..."

This terminology is always written from your perspective. Consider this example Ability description:

"Roll Spirit vs Dexterity against a creature within short range. On a win, the creature takes 2d6 damage. On a loss, half damage."

In this case, you roll Spirit and the creature you chose rolls Dexterity. If you win the Opposed Skill Check, the creature takes 2d6 damage. If you lose the Opposed Skill Check, the creature takes half of that damage. It's YOUR win or loss, always.

MULTIPLE TARGETS

Whenever an Ability indicates multiple targets - for example, "Roll Spirit vs Dexterity against each creature within short range" - that always means that the character invoking the Ability rolls their Skill once and compares that result against each of the targets' roll results, one at a time.

ROUNDING

Unless otherwise stated, always round down when dividing or otherwise modifying values.
